2747.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the root morpheme; prefixes and suffixes (any number of them) never take primary stress. In monomorphemic / unprefixed words this coincides with the word-initial syllable (examples 'bud:a, 'gab:ula, 'yalabana, 'dij:arabaga, 'galab:arab:anda, 2-6 syllables, all initial). Formalised metrically (2.5.1): Rule 1 builds a left-headed binary foot over the first two root syllables, then feet from the margins inwards (penultimate pair, first two prefix syllables); Rule 2 builds a left-headed unbounded tree over the stem (root + suffixes) and a right-headed unbounded tree over the prefix string; word-initial syllabic consonants are extrametrical. Primary stress is accompanied by vowel lengthening.
2747.srule: Secondary stress on the penultimate syllable and on alternating syllables leftward from it (right-to-left), but never on the syllable immediately following the primary-stressed (root-initial) syllable; a polysyllabic prefix string additionally receives a secondary stress on its first syllable (left-headed foot over the first two prefix syllables, Stress Rule 1(b)).

2751.dq: word accent occurs on the head of the rightmost iambic foot. [...] There is an accent retraction process which draws the accent of a word to the left edge of the accentual domain when the word is preceded by another word in the phonological phrase. (pp. 191, 203; data are Mailhot's 1971 elicitations of individual words, p. 202)
2751.dloc: sec. 3.2 'Accent', thesis pp. 190-191 and p. 203; evidence pp. 191-203; restated ch. 4 pp. 243-244.
2751.heavy: syllable weight is determined by vowel length alone: a long vowel forms the nucleus of a heavy syllable and a short vowel forms the nucleus of a light syllable (p. 191); word-final /mʷ/ is the one coda that contributes to syllable weight (pp. 195, 203); /e/ counts as long (p. 191); a short vowel plus glide is assumed to count as long but unconfirmed (p. 196 fn. 124)
2751.dflt: All-light strings are parsed right to left into (L L) iambs and the head of the foot is accented: penult accent when the final syllable is extrametrical (examples 736-743, e.g. 738/742 mət'tʃɨma 'it is near' (L L)<L>, 741/743 kəskʊ'wʊnɨts 'clouds' L (L L)<L>), final accent when it is not (example 723/726 ʌm'mɨʃkʷ 'beaver' (L L), an accented light final syllable). Both outcomes are attested in the source (pp. 194-195, 197-198).
2751.prule: Quantity-sensitive right-edge iambic system: syllables are parsed right to left into iambic feet (L H, L L, or a lone H); word accent falls on the head of the rightmost foot; the final syllable is optionally extrametrical; stray light syllables are left unparsed; heavy = long vowel (codas ignored, except word-final /mʷ/). Net effect: accent on the ultima when the final syllable is not extrametrical (a heavy final as in 713/717 ta:'ha:w 'it is cold'; a light final heading an (L L) iamb as in 723/726 ʌm'mɨʃkʷ 'beaver'; a final made heavy by word-final /mʷ/ as in 724/727 wa:pa:'tum 'he sees'); on the penult when the final syllable is extrametrical and the penult is heavy (729/734 pʌ'ka:hway 'hen') or heads an (L L) iamb (741/743 kəskʊ'wʊnɨts 'clouds'); on the antepenult when the final is extrametrical and the penult is a stray light syllable after a heavy antepenult (744/748 u'ta:kʊʃ/hits 'yesterday', 747/749 tʃəppə'ka:ʃimʊn 'you swim'); never further left than the antepenult (p. 200).

2752.dq: Ударение, как правило, падает на последний слог слова (stress, as a rule, falls on the last syllable of the word); the unstressed items are explicitly 'приименные постпозитивные элементы' (adnominal postpositive elements, i.e. clitics), and Christensen p. 133 §13 separates phrase-level cases: 'l'accentuation ou la non-accentuation d'un mot dans la phrase dépend quelquefois de la diction'.
2752.dloc: Moshkalo 1999, p. 202, 'Farizandi dialekt', section 'Fonologicheskie svedenija', paragraph beginning 'Udarenie' (read); identical sentence p. 198 ('Jaran(d)i dialekt'); group-level rule p. 177 (Rastorgueva & Molchanova 1999). 2752.prule: Word stress falls, as a rule, on the last syllable of the word (quantity-insensitive final stress); exceptions are said to be few but are not listed. Postpositive adnominal elements (ezafe -e, indefinite -(y)e, pronominal enclitics) stand outside the stress domain and never take stress. Translation of the quote: 'Stress, as a rule, falls on the last syllable of the word: ossoxun bone, tariki darkness, vasa hungry, pura boy, son, buga father, mune mother, etc. Exceptions are few. The adnominal postpositive elements do not take stress: 1) the ezafe marker...; 2) the indefiniteness marker -(y)e...; 3) the enclitic pronouns...'
2752.srule: Secondary stress exists but its placement is not given: Christensen 1930 (p. 36) does not mark secondary accent and says only that in these dialects its rules are 'généralement les mêmes que celles du persan littéraire'; Moshkalo 1999 (pp. 198, 202) and Rastorgueva & Molchanova 1999 (p. 177, 'Вопросы ударения в Ц.И.д. не изучены') say nothing about it. Two nearly equal accents (prefix + ending/stem) are heard in Natanzi verb forms with an infixed pronominal clitic (Christensen 1930 p. 247 §11; Farizandi p. 133 §12).

vlen.q: In addition to this basic set of vowel contrasts, Nāti maintains a contrast between long and short vowels in the case of front unrounded and back rounded vowels. 2754.heavy: Long (double) vowels ('perturbation of this pattern by long vowels'); closed syllables with short vowel, initial and non-initial ('closed initial syllable weight', 'a single principle of closed-syllable weight'), operating inconsistently; addendum: 'any heavy syllable (short closed as well as long)'.
2754.dflt: 2nd syllable, then alternating even syllables (1985 text-based account); 2nd syllable only, no alternation beyond it (1990 addendum)
2754.prule: Weight-sensitive Yupik iambic system counted from the left. 1985 text-based account: stress on the 2nd syllable ('fundamentally deuterotonic') and alternate syllables thereafter; a long (double) vowel is stressed wherever it stands and perturbs the count; a closed syllable with short vowel, initial or non-initial, carries a 'balancing' weight that inconsistently attracts stress onto a closed 1st syllable (qántaɣ̣ā́kun, mánti·ɣ̣ámun) or retracts/suppresses the expected stress on the following open syllable. 1990 addendum (one speaker, elicited): stress on any heavy syllable (short closed as well as long); word-level stress on the 2nd syllable if the 1st is not long, plus on the 1st if it is short closed; no alternating stress beyond the 2nd syllable.
2754.srule: Krauss ranks no stress as primary or secondary. 1985 account (Menovshchikov's accent marks + Nututein tape): beyond the 2nd-syllable stress, stress recurs on alternate (even-numbered) syllables rightward (aɣyúqɨqúvɨk 'if you are bored'), long vowels stressed wherever they stand and perturbing the count, closed non-initial syllables inconsistently retracting or suppressing the stress expected on the next open syllable; 'many'/'abundant counterexamples'. 1990 addendum (speaker A. Verbitskaya): alternate-syllable stress inoperative beyond the 2nd syllable ('Stress is quite absent on the fourth and eighth syllables'); other word-internal prominences on heavy syllables (short closed or long).

There are also plenty of instances of perturbation of this pattern by long vowels ... Here, though, the alternate stress operates usually starting on the second syllable, also the one which Menovshchikov more often chooses to note as more prominent, according to the fundamentally deuterotonic pattern. evidence_works.detail: Auditory transcription of stress (no instrumental measurement is mentioned) from Krauss's own elicitation of Antonina Verbitskaya (December 1985, Moscow) and from re-listening to the Nututein and Eqaluk Naukan story tapes. Finds that AV's speech 'lacks the alternate syllable stress common to all AY and CSY' (no stress on the 4th and 8th syllables, 'at -ray- and -rar-', of qìqmíɣarayasùxłurarayáqa 'my nice poor little dog', p. 2), has in that word two stressed syllables 'with raised pitch', the second (word stress) and the second-last ('phrase-final stress (discourse level)'), 'representing the two types of stress (not due to natural weight)', with 'little or no vowel lengthening with stress in open syllables' (p. 2), stress on long vowels and 'prominence also (without raised pitch) on short closed syllables', and that 'The main specific Naukan prosodic trait at word-level is the stress on second syllable'; on the tapes, by contrast, 'The alternate Syllable stress Principle is indeed Present in their speech (e.g. Nututein situxwearumdluku), though not entirely consistently: it appears occasionally to fail'. Krauss marks passages for revision ('(Revise.', p. 2) and closes the phonology section, which he says was originally presented as evidence placing Naukanski outside the Yupik continuum, with 'needs to be revised, to show that these points are rather weak'.

2758.tone: Ndaka is analysed throughout as a two-tone (H/L) Bantu D30 language with floating tones, register/depressor effects and three verb-root tone classes (Ch. 3, pp. 65-121). Stress is mentioned once, in passing and hedged ('I take... to be due more to penultimate word stress than lexical tone', 'the penultimate/accented syllable rise'), as the explanation for a penult pitch rise and final fall on all-Low 2s-past verb forms of every root class (pp. 70, 76, 84); the rise is blocked where a floating H follows (2s/3s-future Rising forms). 2759.idn: Source describes báŋgwà, the speech of Bangoua village (Ndé Division, West Province), classed by the author as a variant of ndà'ndà' (ALCAM 980, Nda'nda' du Nord-Est); not the Fontem Bangwa (Nweh).
2759.tone: Two level tones (haut, bas) contrasting lexically (minimal pairs p. 77: ké 'se promener' vs kè 'porter', dú 'pleuvoir' vs dù 'quitter', tʃɛ́ 'lire' vs tʃɛ̀ 'insulter', nɔ́k 'laisser' vs nɔ̀k 'danser', kák 'assiette' vs kàk 'magie', etc.); monosyllabic nouns and verbs carry only the two schemes H and B (p. 77 a)); two contour tones (montant, descendant) which the author treats as unit tones, not sequences of level tones (p. 76); plus a super-high tone realised above normal H (pp. 76-77). Chumbow & Nguendjio 1991 (JWAL 21, 'Floating tones in Bangwa') add grammatical floating tones, downstep and upstep ('le ton super haut', abstract; downstep, introduction p. 3). 2764.prule: Ndogo is described as a tone language (sec. 5 'Tone', pp. 16-33: four levels 'low, mid, high, very high', p. 17). On accent the author gives only 'suggestions (I shall not call them rules)': monosyllables unproblematic; polysyllables are mostly compounds of monosyllables 'each one of which must have its own accent duly stressed'; among disyllables some have 'an even stress on both syllables' and some 'a real accent on the first' (the latter typically words with l, r, n in the second syllable; with r the second syllable is often lost at the expense of the first: mbòro > mbòò, kóró > kóó); 'the accent usually lies on the first syllable of dissyllables', so reduplicated disyllables carry accents on the 1st and 3rd syllables (exception mbulàmbulà, accent on the 2nd). No fixed, syllable-count-computable stress position is stated.
2764.srule: Not described for simple words in Santandrea 1961 (sec. 4 'Accent' p. 15-16, sec. 5 'Tone' (d) p. 29 read): no secondary or rhythmic stress is mentioned. 2765.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Lexical tone: two basic level tones, high (H, acute) and low (B, grave), borne by the vowel (the tone-bearing mora), plus derived rising (caron) and falling (circumflex) contours. Mosange noun stems (class prefix excluded) attest the surface schemes H (li-só 'œil'), B (wo 'toi'), H-H (li-tálé 'pierre'), H-B (li-fúfa 'poumon'), B-B (li-bongu 'marché'), B-H (li-bɔkɛ́ 'courge'), B-B-B (e-ngombela 'panier'), B-B-H (solokó 'antilope') and B-H-B (kambéli 'chèvre'); no rising-tone and no falling-tone monosyllabic stems, and no H-H-H, H-B-B or H-H-B trisyllabic stems in the corpus (the lists for the two remaining trisyllabic schemes, B-H-H (59) and H-B-H (64), likewise contain no Mosange form; H-B-H 'ne semble être attesté que dans les langues du groupe du nord-est du fleuve Congo', to which Mosange does not belong). Vowel length is not distinctive (p. 44).

2765.tone: The source says nothing about stress or accent for Mosange or any of the ten languages. A full-text search of the whole thesis text (20,240 lines) for accent|stress|intensit|proémin|pénulti|tonique|emphase|prominen|accentu hits only ('accent aigu' / 'accent grave' as the names of the tone diacritics, p. 62), a wordlist gloss 'os proéminent des yeux', and the bibliography title Philippson 1991 'Tons et Accent'. What it does state: two level tones H and B with rising and falling contours; the vowel is the tone-bearing mora 'dans presque toutes les langues à l'étude' (syllabic consonants as tone bearers are mentioned only for the regional language Zamba, Kamanda 1991, p. 62); surface tone schemes on noun stems listed per language pp. 63-67, with 16 schemes over mono-, di- and trisyllabic stems in all (p. 67); Mosange belongs to the subgroup (libóbi, mondóngó, monyɔ́ngɔ, mosángé, plus págáɓéte) with no falling tone on monosyllabic stems (p. 64); no distinctive vowel length (p. 44); 7-vowel system (p. 44). The tonology section is explicitly a preliminary surface inventory ('démarche préliminaire', p. 62); De Boeck 1951's five-way typology of regional tone systems is quoted but not applied to Mosange.

2766.prule: Lexical (unpredictable) primary stress: final, penultimate and antepenultimate stress all occur and are contrastive (minimal pairs commò/comme, capille/capillò, léttera/lettera, bomba/bombò, mànna/mannà); stress is confined to the last three syllables of the word (cannot fall beyond the antepenult), with a strong general preference for penultimate (paroxytone) stress; enclitic pronouns that would push stress beyond the antepenult trigger a systematic rightward shift to the penult of the host+clitic group, with strengthening (gemination) of that syllable's coda.

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article tests whether Coratino's stress-conditioned vowel reduction transfers to nonce words: the seven-vowel system holds only under stress, unstressed non-initial vowels reduce (high to /ɨ/, mid to /ə/) unless word-initial, /a/, or protected by a like-articulated consonant, and diminutive suffixes always take the stress off the root. It gives no rule for main-stress position, so it adds a phonetic correlate of stress (reduction of unstressed vowels) and affix stress for the Apulian variety of Corato, not a placement rule for the catalog's Neapolitan record, which rests on Ledgeway 2009.

2771.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word, stated with no weight or vowel-length condition (long vowels a:, i:, u: are listed as phonemes on p. 1 and p. 16 but play no part in the rule); the p. 16 summary makes it categorical: 'Primary syllable stress always occurs on first syllable of the word.'
2771.srule: In words of more than three syllables a secondary stress 'generally' falls on the third syllable (yulparira 'south' -> "yulpa-'rira); three-syllable words have the initial stress only (kú-tjara); further secondary stresses in longer words are not described.
2771.quote: SECTION 3. STRESS OR ACCENT. A. SYLLABLE STRESS. The FIRST syllable of each word is stressed (or accented). E.g. kutjara 'two' is pronounced kú - tjara.
